text: Before there was a Hyde Park, before there were street numbers, there was prairie and marsh sloping down to the lake.
Sand ridges with bur oaks.
Swales of wildflowers.
A grassland that ran flat to the horizon.
The water was close, and the ground stayed wet most of the year.
None of it was empty.
This was Potawatomi land, held in common with the Ojibwe and the Odawa in an alliance called the Council of Three Fires.
The three nations traced their council, by one elder's reckoning from the old scrolls, back to the 790s, near the straits of Michilimackinac.
They divided the work between them.
The Ojibwe kept the faith.
The Odawa kept the trade.
The Potawatomi kept the fire.
They had lived, hunted, and traded along these shores for generations before any deed existed to describe them.
The water was the reason any of this mattered to outsiders.
A few miles northwest of here ran the Chicago Portage, a low seven-mile stretch of wet ground that flooded into a shallow expanse the traders called Mud Lake.
In a wet season you could float a canoe from the Great Lakes almost to the Mississippi, with only a short carry between the two watersheds.
People had used that crossing for centuries.
In the summer of 1673, Kaskaskia guides led a French fur trader, Louis Jolliet, and a Jesuit priest, Jacques Marquette, back up the Illinois and the Des Plaines and over that portage.
They were the first Europeans known to stand on the site of Chicago.
Jolliet saw at once that a single short canal could join the lake to the river, and the whole interior of the continent to the sea.
It took 175 years for anyone to dig it.
